name: Employment surgery

lead: Employment surgery refers to cosmetic procedures, commonly eyelid surgery or nose work, done before job hunting to improve appearance on a resume photo or in interviews. It is discussed most in South Korea, where appearance is widely seen as a factor in hiring.

Surveys and press reports describe it as common enough that cosmetic surgery is sometimes given as a graduation gift. Wikipedia notes that more attractive applicants are statistically more likely to be hired.

paras: Applicants typically consult a clinic before graduation or before application season, choose one or more procedures, and allow healing time before photos and interviews. Details are medical and procedure-specific.

Surgical risks include complications and dissatisfaction. In South Korea, a reported practice of unlicensed substitutes operating under anesthesia ("ghost surgery") led to a 2021 requirement for operating-room cameras.

chain: Procedure alters eyelids, nose or contour
More conventionally attractive photo and in-person look
angle.text: People use procedures such as eyelid or nose surgery to look more polished for resume photos and interviews, on the belief that attractiveness helps hiring.

lead: Employment surgery is cosmetic surgery sought to gain an edge in job hiring. Appearance is seen as important in South Korea's competitive job market, which Wikipedia says pressures some candidates to have procedures, according to a 2017 Los Angeles Times report [1].

Supporters point to the link between attractiveness and hiring odds. A 2006 survey cited by Wikipedia found 92.2 percent of South Korean women expected appearance-based discrimination in interviews, and 80 percent of public companies asked for personal information including photos [1].
Cosmetic surgery has also become a common graduation gift, per The New Yorker in 2015 [1].

paras: Gallup Korea data cited by Wikipedia show support for plastic surgery before marriage rising from 38 percent in 1994 to 66 percent in 2015, and the share of women reporting surgery rising from 5 to 31 percent [1]. A 2020 Statista survey found nearly 25 percent of women aged 19-29 had procedures versus 2 percent of men [1].

Ghost surgeries, where unlicensed substitutes operate while the patient is under anesthesia, were estimated by the Korean Society of Plastic Surgeons to have affected about 100,000 people from 2008 to 2014; about five patients died in such operations from 2014 to 2022, per the New York Times [1]. Lawmakers mandated operating-room cameras in 2021 [1]. Critics link beauty standards to lower self-esteem and anxiety, and the show Let Me In was shut down in 2015 after criticism [1].

timeline.event: Reporting describes cosmetic surgery as a graduation gift; Let Me In shut down [1]
Operating-room cameras mandated in South Korea [1]
